2) Implications and Recommendations
Strengthening Policy Support to Resolve the Digital Divide
● Closing the Digital Skills Gap Although the digital literacy of older generations is rapidly improving, there is still a noticeable gap
compared to younger generations.⇒ Digital education programs for older adults and digitally excluded groups must be strengthened to
improve their ability to use digital devices and services.
● The Impact of Digital Literacy on the Adoption of New Technologies Basic digital literacy skills play a critical role in adapting to and
leveraging new technologies such as AI, VR, and AR.⇒ As new technologies continue to expand and the digital landscape rapidly
evolves, it is essential to provide age-and skill-appropriate digital education to enhance technology adoption.
Institutional Support for Digital Economy Expansion
● Building Infrastructure to Expand Simple Payment Simple payment is a catalyst for the growth of the digital economy.
⇒ Promoting digital economy activation by supporting the establishment of system infrastructure (QR code, NFC, etc.) for the spread of
simple payment.
● Strengthening Security Measures for Safe Digital Finance The use of digital financial services such as simple payment and Internet
banking continues to increase.
⇒ Preventative measures and educational programs must be implemented to address risks such as hacking and online financial fraud.
● Regulatory Measures for Safe International Direct Purchase As International direct purchase platforms enter the Korean market, the use
of International direct purchase for online shopping is steadily increasing.
⇒ Support for personal information protection and payment process security for a safe and reliable International direct purchase
experience.
● Protecting the Digitally Disadvantaged Groups The use of digital finance and e-commerce is growing significantly among older adults
and digitally disadvantaged populations.
⇒ Need to provide digital financial education to protect the digitally disadvantaged.
Establishing Trust and Ethics Guidelines in the Shift to AI
● Increased Use of AI to Improve Information Reliability As AI services expand, the number of users is also increasing.
⇒ Developing measures to increase the reliability of information generated by AI and prevent misinformation and AI illusions.
● Establishing Ethical Standards and Increasing Transparency in AI Services
⇒ Developing educational programs and guidelines to prevent ethical issues arising from AI services, including generative AI.
⇒ Strengthening transparency regarding the collection, use, and transfer of personal information within AI services.
● Supporting AI Technology Education Overall perceptions and evaluations of AI technology are on the decline, with people who have
experience with AI evaluating it more positively than those who have not.
⇒ Improving AI literacy by expanding AI technology experience opportunities and providing customized education for all age groups.

1) Five-Year Trends in Digital Utilization Capabilities
● Since the 2020s, digital devices incorporating new technologies―such as VR/AR devices and AI-powered smartphones―
have continuously evolved and become more widespread.
● As a result, the importance of digital utilization competencies, which enable individuals to understand and utilize new
technologies effectively, has grown. Analyzing changes and disparities in digital utilization competencies is crucial for
identifying and supporting groups struggling to adapt to the rapidly changing digital landscape.
● By conducting a time-series analysis of digital utilization competencies from 2020 to 2024, this study aims to classify
digital utilization competence into basic and intermediate competencies. It will examine trends in changes by age group
and identify generational differences, ultimately aiming to deriving policy implications.
Overall, digital utilization capabilities are improving. ‘Creating presentation materials using
Hangul, PowerPoint, etc.’ increased by 11.0%p compared to 2020.

● From 2020 to 2024, overall digital utilization competencies have shown an increasing trend. Notably, ‘Creating presentation
materials using Hangul, PowerPoint, etc.’ showed the largest increase, rising by 11.0%p compared to 2020. Meanwhile,
tasks such as ‘Copying/moving files and folders’ remained at similar levels or slightly declined.
● Significant improvements were also observed in other areas. ‘Verifying the reliability of information found online’ increased
by 10.1%p compared to 2021, ‘Setting security measures for devices or accounts’ rose by 8.9%p, and ‘Adjusting settings to
prevent excessive exposure of personal information’ grew by 6.5%p.
2) Five-Year Trends in Basic and Intermediate Digital Competencies
Both basic and intermediate digital competencies showed an upward trend, with intermediate
competencies increasing by 7.5 percentage points compared to 2020.

devices’.
● The proportion of individuals capable of intermediate-level competencies, including ‘Using basic formulas in Excel’,
‘Connecting and installing new devices’, and ‘Creating presentation materials with Hangul, PowerPoint, etc.’ showed a
strong upward trend, increasing by 7.5%p compared to 2020.

● By age group, over 90% of individuals under 40 years old were found to have basic digital competencies. Meanwhile,
88.3% of those in their 50s, 81.6% in their 60s, and 69.1% of those aged 70 and older demonstrated basic competencies,
highlighting generational differences.
● However, when comparing the growth rates since 2020, basic digital competencies in the 50s age group increased by
8.2%p, and in the 60s age group by 11.1%p, showing the largest improvements. This trend suggests that generational gaps
in digital competencies are expected to narrow over time.

● Intermediate digital competencies have also been on a continuous increase since 2020. Those in their 20s (87.7%) and 30s

growth trend in the middle-aged and older adults.

Implications and Recommendations
● Rapid Growth in Internet Security, Reliability, and Personal Data Competencies
Online security, reliability, and privacy capabilities have improved significantly since 2021.
⇒ Users are becoming increasingly aware of security concerns when using digital devices and the Internet.
● The Digital Literacy of Older Adults Is Growing Rapidly, but Gaps Still Exist.
Although the digital capabilities of older generations are rapidly improving, there is still a significant gap compared to
younger generations who are more familiar with digital environments.
⇒ Various support and educational policies are needed to help older adults adapt to the fast-evolving digital
landscape.
● Strengthening Digital Competency Education for the Digitally Disadvantaged
Various digital competence education programs are currently being implemented to support digitally marginalized
groups, including ‘Digital Learning Center’, ‘Mobile Bus Services’1), ‘Hangul Sunshine Bus’2), and ‘Seoul Digital
Companion Plaza’3).
⇒ Therefore, in order to further strengthen the digital capabilities of the elderly, it is essential to continuously support
and strengthen existing policies and programs, develop customized educational content, improve accessibility to
digital education, and establish a sustainable support system through institutional frameworks.
1) ‘Digital Learning Center’ is a policy led by the Ministry of Science and ICT and the National Information Society Agency (NIA), which has established
911 centers nationwide in welfare facilities, community centers, libraries, and other locations. Since April 2021, the ‘Mobile Bus Service’ project has
been expanded to all cities and provinces, helping to reduce regional digital gaps.
2) ‘Hangul Sunshine Bus’ is a project promoted by the Ministry of Education's Lifelong Learning Support Division, utilizing a mobile education bus to
provide digital literacy training for marginalized groups, such as older adults. The program teaches how to use kiosk, delivery and shopping apps, etc.
3) ‘Seoul Digital Companion Plaza’ is a facility operated by the Seoul Metropolitan Government, offering digital education and counseling to improve
digital competencies among older adults.

become easier to purchase products or services by linking your credit/debit card or bank account.
The rate of use of simple payment has increased compared to 2020,
and the increase was greatest in older age groups.

Implications and Recommendations
● Simple Payments as a Catalyst for Digital Economy Activation
Users of simple payment make more frequent online shopping purchases and spend more on average per month than non-
users.
⇒ The introduction, popularization, spread, and increased use of simple payment technologies are playing a key role in
activating the digital economy.
⇒ In order to activate the digital economy, the expansion of simple payment services and the necessary policy support are
essential.
※ Support in needed for infrastructure development (QR codes, NFC, etc.) to expand simple payment.
● Strengthening Prevention and Protection for Inclusive Digital Finance
As the number of users of simple payment and Internet banking increases, the need for education and protection against
digital financial risks also increases.
⇒ Need to establish policies and education programs to prevent risks such as voice phishing and electronic financial fraud.
⇒ Need to strengthen policies to protect user personal information and ensure safe digital finance.

Implications and Recommendations
● Trend in the Increase of International Direct Purchase
As International direct purchase platforms such as Amazon, AliExpress, and Temu enter the Korean market, opportunities for
International direct purchase have expanded. Younger generations who are more familiar with these platforms are actively
participating in International direct purchase.
● Strengthening Consumer Protection for Safe International Direct Purchase
As International direct purchases continue to increase, the need to resolve various issues that may arise is growing.
⇒ Establishing of consumer protection standards and policies for international payment and shipping processes.
⇒ Creating a safe International direct purchasing environment by protecting consumer personal information and ensuring
product quality and safety.
⇒ Efforts to raise awareness of safe International direct purchase methods and consumer information protection

Implications and Recommendations
● Trend in the Increase of Subscription Service Use
The increase in subscription service use appears to be driven by changing consumer trends that prioritize experiences over
ownership, the emergence of new technology-based subscription services, and the introduction of low-cost subscription
plans.
● Strengthening Consumer Protection for Subscription Services
As the number of users of subscription services increases, the need to protect consumers from issues such as ‘dark patterns’ 4)
and inconvenient cancellation procedures is growing.
⇒ Strengthening consumer education on subscription service automatic payment methods and cancellation procedures.
⇒ Establishing guidelines for canceling and renewing subscription services and recurring payments.
4) In subscription services, dark patterns can include insufficient prior notice of price hikes or renewing subscriptions without providing proper
cancellation instructions.

Implicationas and Recommendations
● Trend in the Increase of Internet Banking Use
It was found that both younger age groups (ages 12 to 19) and older age groups (60 and over) are becoming accustomed to
Internet banking, while those in their 20s to 40s are already familiar with it.
● Growth of Internet-Only Banks and Simple Transfer Services
The influence of simple transfer services provided by popular platforms such as KakaoTalk and Naver is expanding, and
Internet-only banks such as Toss Bank and K Bank are also actively expanding their services.
⇒ In contrast, the use of traditional bank services has declined.
● Digital Financial Education and Security Measures
New security risks such as digital financial fraud and personal information leaks.
⇒ Expanding support to ensure the security and reliability of digital financial services.
⇒ Expanding digital financial education to strengthen consumer protection

⇒ AI services are becoming increasingly integrated into our daily lives.

Implications and Recommendations
● Concerns about AI's shortcomings are growing
Public awareness and overall evaluation of AI services have declined compared to the previous year.
⇒ Recent issues such as personal information leakage and information reliability issues due to hallucination5) appear to be
affecting perceptions of AI services.
● Experienced Users View AI Services More Positively than Non-Users
As AI services become more deeply embedded in our daily lives, people who have experienced them tend to perceive them
as increasingly ‘essential’ services and evaluate them positively.
● Strengthening AI Service Reliability and Transparency, and Supporting Education
⇒ Establishing guidelines to address misinformation and AI hallucinations.
⇒ Developing of ethical guidelines and monitoring system for collection, use, and application of personal information by AI
⇒ Increasing social acceptance and creating a more inclusive AI-centric society by expanding AI-related education and
experiences
5) Hallucination: A term meaning "illusion" or "auditory hallucination" in English. In the context of AI, it refers to instances where language models like
ChatGPT generate plausible but false or misleading information.

Implications and Recommendations
● Digital Utilization Capabilities and Introduction of New Technologies
Existing digital literacy skills play a critical role in introducing and applying new digital technologies.
⇒ As we transition into the AI era, it is essential to have a solid understanding and capabilities in AI technology.
● Strengthening Education to Enhance Digital Utilization Capabilities
Improving digital literacy is a fundamental step toward understanding and effectively leveraging AI.
⇒ Support for AI and digital literacy education.
⇒ Implementation of customized AI education programs for the elderly and digitally vulnerable

(cid:13000)(cid:13143)(cid:2)(cid:231)(cid:742)(cid:690)(cid:806)(cid:487)(cid:824)(cid:2)(cid:177)(cid:806)(cid:487)(cid:690)(cid:806)(cid:568)(cid:487)(cid:811)
● Population: Households and population aged 3 or older nationwide
● Subject: 25,000 households and members aged 3 or older in the household nationwide
● Valid Sample: 25,509 households and 60,229 household members aged 3 or older in the household
● Survey Method: Home visit interview survey
● Survey Period: Sep 23, 2024 ~ Nov 22, 2024
● Reference Date: July 1, 2024
● Sampling: Stratified Multi-stage Cluster Sampling
● Estimation: Post-stratification (Application of stratified multi-stage cluster sampling estimation formula)
- Household: Estimated households for 2024 in Household Projections by KOSTAT
- Household member: Estimated population for 2024 in Population Projections by KOSTAT
● Sampling Error
- Household: Internet access rate ± 0.02%p (95% confidence level)
- Household member: Internet use rate ± 0.18%p (95% confidence level)
Sampling Design
● Target Household Allocation: 25,000 households are first allocated to the 17 cities and provinces in proportion to the
square root of the estimated number of households in 2024, and then further allocated within each city/province
to each dong, eup, and myeon in proportion to the number of households based on the 2022 registration census
microdata.
● Household Sampling: Using the general household survey wards from the 2022 Registration Census Microdata
(Statistics Korea) as the sampling frame, 3,000 survey wards were systematically sampled after allocating the
sample proportionally to the square root of the number of survey wards in each of the 17 regional clusters. Then, 8
to 9 households were statistically sampled from each selected survey ward.

Household Internet Access Rate and Number of Internet-Accessing Households
99.97% of Korean households have access to the Internet
As of July 2024, the percentage of households with Internet access remained unchanged from the previous year, at
99.97% of the total 22,267 thousand households. The number of households with Internet access reached approximately
22,261 thousand, an increase of about 373 thousand households compared to the previous year.

Personal Internet Usage Rate and Number of Users
94.5% of the population aged 3 or older are ‘Internet users’
As of July 2024, the proportion of Internet users (a person who has used the Internet within the last month) among
the population aged 3 or older (51,020 thousand persons) was 94.5% (48,189 thousand persons), an increase of 0.5%p
(approximately 442,000 people) from the previous year.

Internet Usage rate is highest among people in their ‘20s’ (99.6%)

Internet Usage Rate and Number of Users by Region
The region with the highest Internet Usage rate is ‘Daegu’ (97.5%) and the region with the lowest Internet
Usage rate is ‘Gangwon’ (88.9%)
Looking at the Internet Usage rate for each of 17 regions, ‘Daegu’ (97.5%), ‘Daejeon’ (97.2%), ‘Gwangju’ (96.0%), and
‘Chungbuk’ (96.0%) showed relatively high usage rates, while ‘Jeju’ (92.2%), ‘Jeonnam’ (91.4%), and ‘Gangwon’ (88.9%)

PART.5
Internet Usage Frequency and Hours
90.5% of Internet users use the Internet at least once a day, and the average usage time per
week is 20.5 hours
Among the Internet users aged 3 or older, 90.5% use the Internet at least once a day, and the average usage time per week
was 20.5 hours, a decrease of 0.3 hours from the previous year. Additionally, 65.2% of people used the Internet for more
than 14 hours per week on average (19.0% for ‘14 hours-under 21 hours’, 26.1% for ‘21 hours-under 35 hours’, 20.0% for ‘35
hours or more’).

(cid:49)(cid:66)(cid:83)(cid:85)(cid:15)(cid:21)(cid:3006)(cid:3006)(cid:42)(cid:15)(cid:3006)(cid:52)(cid:86)(cid:83)(cid:87)(cid:70)(cid:90)(cid:3006)(cid:48)(cid:87)(cid:70)(cid:83)(cid:87)(cid:74)(cid:70)(cid:88)
(cid:13000)(cid:13143)(cid:2)(cid:231)(cid:742)(cid:690)(cid:806)(cid:487)(cid:824)(cid:2)(cid:177)(cid:450)(cid:587)(cid:487)(cid:459)(cid:721)(cid:568)(cid:806)(cid:487)
As Internet spreads rapidly throughout society, it is becoming more important to examine the specific Internet use
patterns and Internet use in everyday life, as well as the social impact of the Internet, in addition to the quantitative
growth of the Internet Usage rate and the number of users.
This survey aims to examine the rapidly changing Internet use environment and pattern changes to provide statistics that
can be utilized in various fields like government policy and business strategy establishment, academic research, etc.
Specific objectives of this survey are as follows:
(cid:18363) Quantitative measurement of Internet users and usage rates in Korea
(cid:18363) Providing basic data to calculate the ICT statistical index and the international index of international organization
(cid:18363) Analyzing the Internet usage environment in households like ICT device ownership, Internet access, etc.
(cid:18363) Understanding the Internet use patterns for time, place, method, purpose, etc.
(cid:18363) Analyzing the Internet use in daily life and the impact of the Internet
(cid:18363) Future intention for using the Internet
(cid:13001)(cid:13143)(cid:2)(cid:231)(cid:742)(cid:690)(cid:806)(cid:487)(cid:824)(cid:2)(cid:110)(cid:568)(cid:705)(cid:721)(cid:643)(cid:690)(cid:824)
▶ October 1999
Conducted the “Study on Estimating the Number of Internet Users in Korea and Verifying Statistical Techniques” that
targeted 1,403 households nationwide (3,445 persons from the population aged 7 or older)
- Internet user is defined as ‘someone that uses the Internet once or more a month on average’
▶ March 2000
Conducted the “Study on Estimating the Number of Internet Users for the First Half of 2020 and Verifying and Improving Statistical
Techniques” that targeted 2,623 households nationwide (8,491 persons from the population aged 7 or older)
▶ August 2000 ­ December 2000
Conducted the “Survey On the Number of Internet Users and Internet Usage Behavior”
- Established a survey panel that targeted about 3,500 households nationwide (about 10,000 persons from the
population aged 7 or older)
- Changed the survey method to a telephone survey after establishing the survey panel in August 2000 (interview
survey) (However, interview survey was carried out in parallel for new samples)
▶ March 2001 ­ December 2001
Conducted the “Survey On the Number of Internet Users and Internet Usage Behavior”
- Conducted telephone surveys that targeted identical survey panel households four times annually (March, June,
September, December)

- Changed the definition of the Internet user to ‘someone who has used the Internet at least once within the last month’
- Also included the wireless Internet users who get access through the mobile communication network as Internet users

This survey was designed to understand the current status and patterns of Internet use, the Internet environment of
households, the current status of Internet use in daily life, and the social impact of the Internet. It was also designed to
predict future trends through time series analysis with past survey results.
Major contents of this survey are as follows:
(cid:18363) Calculation and time series analysis of the number of Internet users and the usage rate
(cid:18363) Calculation of the number of mobile Internet and smartphone Internet users and the usage rate
(cid:18363) Internet usage status by gender, age, education, occupation, region, etc.
(cid:18363) Internet usage pattern like Internet use time, frequency, place, purpose, etc.
(cid:18363) Internet usage environment like ICT device ownership, household Internet access. etc.
(cid:18363) Internet communication status like email, instant messenger, SNS, etc.
(cid:18363) Internet economic activity status like Online Shopping, Internet banking, etc.
(cid:18363) Media use status via online for TV, newspaper, radio, magazine, book, etc.
(cid:18363) Analysis of reasons for not using the Internet and future intentions of use

● Internet Access Rate
Ratio of households that can access the Internet through the wired Internet, wireless LAN, mobile Internet, etc. among
all households, regardless of actual use
● Computer Ownership Rate
Ratio of households that own a computer like a desktop PC, a laptop, a smart pad, etc. among all households, regardless
of actual use
● Internet User (Usage Rate)
(Ratio of) persons in the population aged 3 or older who have used the Internet within the last month
● Mobile Internet User (Usage Rate)
(Ratio of) Internet users who have used the Internet within the last month via a mobile device that can connect to the
Internet wirelessly, like a mobile phone, a smartphone, a smart pad, a wearable device, etc.
● Smartphone User (Usage Rate)
(Ratio of) Internet users who have used the Internet via a smartphone within the last month

● Wearable Device
A device that is worn on the body in the form of a watch, glasses, apparel, etc., collects information of the surrounding

- Wearable Device User (Usage Rate): (Ratio of) Internet users aged 12 or older who own a wearable device and have

A service that enables individuals to send and receive data like messages, photos, etc. online by using a computer, a
smartphone, etc. in real time
- Instant Messenger User (Usage Rate): (Ratio of) Internet users aged 6 or older who have used an instant messenger
within the last year
● SNS (Social Networking Service)
An activity for sharing communication and information by reinforcing personal relationships with acquaintances like
friends, colleagues, etc. or by forming a new personal network on the Internet, and also includes the act of simply
perusing or observing contents posted by others
- SNS User (Usage Rate): (Ratio of) Internet users aged 6 or older who have used SNS within the last year

(Ratio of) Internet users aged 6 or older who have used email within the last year

Includes all bank transaction activities like savings, transfer, investment, asset management, etc., and also includes

- Internet Banking User (Usage Rate): (Ratio of) Internet users aged 12 or older who have used Internet banking within

A service that saves media files (photos, music, etc.) and personal files (documents, address book, etc.) in a web server
rather than in an external storage. Stored files can be downloaded to a PC, a smartphone, etc. to carry out desired
operations like editing, etc.
- Cloud Service User (Usage Rate): (Ratio of) Internet users aged 12 or older who have used cloud service within the last
year

● Household Stratification and Sample Allocation
- After stratifying the country into 17 cities and provinces, the target number of households (25,000 households) were
proportionally allocated to the square root based on the number of households (2022 Registration Census) in each city
and province
※ When allocating proportionally for each city and province, square root proportional allocation was used since there was a large possibility
that a problem in representativeness of sample households may occur due to the fact that a large number of sample households will
be allocated to Seoul and Gyeonggi while the number of households allocated to areas such as Sejong, Jeju and Ulsan will be small if
proportional allocation is carried out for each city and province
- Secondary: To reflect the increasing trend of single-person households, after 17 cities and provinces were stratified
into single-person households and multi-person households (2022 Registration Census), the households were
allocated proportionally via square root
- Tertiary: After 17 cities and provinces were stratified into Dong/Eup and Myeon, and the second allocation target
households are allocated in proportion to the number of households in each Dong/Eup and Myeon (2022 Registration
Census)
- Quaternary: The allocated target households for each of the 17 cities and provinces, each number of household
members, and each Dong/Eup and Myeon were converted into the number of Enumeration Districts (ED), and the
required number of survey districts was calculated for each region based on an average of 8.33 households per survey
district.
● Sampling
- ED Sampling: For sampling the standard ED for each Dong/Eup and Myeon in each cluster in each region, systematic
sampling was carried out by utilizing PROC SURVEYSELECT in SAS.
- Household Sampling: Systematic sampling of sample households was conducted using the household registers of
each ED from which the sample was drawn (8-9 households per ED, 8.33 households on average).
- Household Member Sampling: All household members aged 3 or older in the sampled households were surveyed.

A. Fieldwork Overview
● Survey Period
：Sep. 23 ~ Nov. 22, 2024
● Survey Reference Date
：July 1, 2024
● Survey Interval
：1 year
● Survey Target
: Households selected as sample and all members aged 3 or older residing in the household
- However, military servicemen, long-term business travelers and visitors, dormitory residents, inmates, etc. are
excluded
● Survey Method
: Home visit interview survey in which trained interviewers visit the sample households and record the responses to the
questionnaire
● Survey Procedure
: Home visit interview survey by the interviewer ⇒ Management and control by the supervisor in each region ⇒
Questionnaire aggregation ⇒ Supplementary survey and re-survey ⇒ Final data verification
B. Sample Management
● Enumeration District (ED) Management
- In principle, the survey is conducted on EDs sampled in advance. If the survey cannot be conducted due to
redevelopment, natural disaster, etc., the ED within the same cluster closest to the ED in question is used as a
substitute survey target.
● Household Management
- In principle, the survey is conducted targeting EDs sampled in advance. If the survey cannot be conducted due to
long-term absence of household members, strong refusal to respond, etc., the survey is replaced with a preliminary
sample (replacement households) of equivalent EDs sampled with the same household characteristics as the original
household characteristics sampled in the first survey.

A. Data Verification and Substitution
● Data Verification during the Fieldwork Process
- The field supervisor in each region randomly selects at least 30% of the returned questionnaires and conduct a phone
call to confirm whether the interviewer visited and the accuracy of the responses.
- The questionnaires that have passed the fieldwork supervisor’s primary verification are verified for the second time by
a computer program during the editing and entry process.
- The entered data is verified for the third time by an internal validation program during the data processing step.
- For questionnaires that failed each validation step, supplementary survey and re-survey are conducted.
● Data Verification during the Analysis Process
- Time-series comparison and verification is carried out on the average value for each identical group (gender, age,
region, education, occupation, household income, etc.) and the result or previous surveys.
● Non-response Processing Method
- In case a unit non-response, revisit the relevant household at least 3 times or more to collect the response. When
unavoidable, replace the household according to the sample substitution standard and eliminate the unit non-response.
- During field surveys, the occurrence of non-response to items must be minimized. When unavoidable, process ‘Do not
know/no response’ as ‘Other’.
- Non-response to respondent characteristics (education, occupation, household income, etc.) is not corrected.
B. Data Entry and Analysis
● The collected data is entered into the computer through an encoding process, and the data that has finally passed the
multilevel verification process is analyzed by using SPSS for Windows (statistical package program).
- Information that can identify individuals like name, address, and phone number are encoded into a serial number or
excluded during data entry.
● Analysis Unit: Household and Household Member
- Household Independent Variables: Age of the householder, household income and region
- Household Member Independent Variables: Gender, age, gender x age, education level, occupation, household income,
size of region and region
● In order to estimate Internet usage rates, usage rates by gender, age, and region were calculated after estimating
the number of Internet users. For usage rate by occupation and by education level, for which there is no population
information, the usage rate was calculated without estimating the number of Internet users.

The target population for the 2024 Survey on the Internet Usage is defined as the population aged 3 years or older residing in
each household nationwide, and the distribution by region, gender, and age is as shown in <Table 1-6> below. The size of the
target population is 51,020,511 persons, and of these 25,503,193 are males and 25,517,318 are females. By age, those in their
50s are the most with 8,705,899 persons (17.1%), followed by 7,852,297 persons (15.4%) in their 40s, 7,720,341 persons (15.1%)
in their 60s, 6,913,023 persons (13.5%) in their 30s, 6,428,985 persons (12.6%) in their 70s, and 6,372,432 persons (12.5%) in
their 20s. Meanwhile, those in their 10s accounted for 4,546,494 people (8.9%), and those aged 3-9 accounted for 2,481,040
people (4.9%), representing a relatively smaller proportion.

C. Internet Usage Rate and Number of Internet Users by Age
In Korea, the Internet usage rate is highest among those in their teens to 50s, while those aged ‘3-9’ and those in their
‘60s’ also showed high usage rates of 92.0% and 95.7%, respectively. The usage rate for those ‘70+’ was lower than that
of other age groups, but it increased by 3.6%p from the previous year, reaching a usage rate of 68.0%.

D. Internet Usage Rate and Number of Users by Region
Looking at the Internet usage rates of the 17 cities and provinces across the country, ‘Daegu’ (97.5%), ‘Daejeon’ (97.2%),
‘Gwangju’ and ‘Chungbuk’ (each 96.0%), ‘Gyeonggi’ (95.8%) and ‘Sejong’ (95.6%) showed a high Internet Usage rate at
and over 95.0%, followed by ‘Ulsan’ (94.9%), ‘Incheon’ (94.8%), ‘Jeonbuk’ (94.4%), ‘Seoul’ (94.1%), ‘Busan’ (93.4%), and
‘Gyeongnam’ (93.1%). The region with the lowest Internet Usage rate, Gangwon, still recorded 88.9%, indicating that
most local governments had an Internet Usage rate of over 90.0%. ‘Gyeonggi’ had the largest number of Internet users
at 13,061 thousand persons, followed by ‘Seoul’ with 8,728 thousand persons and ‘Busan’ with 3,013 thousand persons.

G. Internet Usage Rate by Household Income
By household income, the Internet Usage rate was highest for households with an average monthly household income
of ‘KRW 5 million or more’, at 97.9%. In contrast, the Internet Usage rate of those with ‘Less than KRW 2 million’ was the
lowest at 73.2%, indicating that as the household income increases, the Internet Usage rate increases.

A. Internet Access Method
It was found that the wireless access methods are used more frequently than wired (68.1%) when accessing the
Internet. Among the wireless Internet access methods, ‘Used wireless Internet within a certain range like Wi-Fi, etc.’
was the highest at 84.7%, followed by ‘Used wireless Internet via a 5G smartphone’ (68.2%), ‘Used wireless Internet via
a 3G/LTE smartphone’ (40.7%), and ‘Used wireless Internet via a portable wireless Internet router (egg), etc.’(5.1%).

G. Activities for Safe Internet Use
About 61.4% of Internet users aged 12 years old were taking measures for the safe use of Internet. Among the detailed
activities, ‘Non-consent to provision of personal information for the purpose of receiving advertising information’ was the
highest at 38.8%, followed by ‘Restriction of access to location data’ (32.8%) and ‘Restriction of access such as keeping
SNS profiles private’ (26.6%).

A. Online Shopping Usage Rate
78.6% of Internet users aged 12 or older are ‘Internet shoppers’ who have purchased products or services (including
reservations and advance purchases) through the Internet within the past year. And, it was found that 22.6% used it
for ‘Within the last 24 hours’, 21.5% for ‘More than 24 hours - within 1 week’, 24.3% for ‘More than 1 week - within 1
month’, and finally, 7.8% for ‘More than 1 month - within 1 year’.

What is Online Shopping?
It refers to purchase products or services through various Online Shopping malls or Internet platforms (site/
application) without visiting stores directly, and includes used transactions, purchasing contents, etc.
(includes using general shopping sites, shopping through instant messengers, shopping through SNS links,
shopping through live commerce platforms, using subscription services/freelancer markets/crowdfunding sites/
apps, etc.)
Example) Naver Shopping, Coupang, 11th Street, Ticketlink, Kakao Talk Gift, Instagram Shops, Kakao Shopping
Live, Kukka, Soomgo, Wadiz, etc.

I. Reasons for Not Using Online Shopping
More than half (53.7%) of non-users of online shopping aged 12 or older cited 'Not interested or needing it' as the main
reason. This was followed by ‘Since buying directly at the store is preferred’ (49.7%), ‘No confidence in using it or do not
know how to use it’ (27.5%), ‘Since the payment process is complicated and inconvenient’ (26.4%), etc.

J. Experience in Selling Products or Services
It was found that 47.6% of Internet users aged 3 or older have experience selling products or services online, including
second-hand transactions. By age group, those in their ‘20s’ showed the highest rate at 72.6%, followed by ‘30s’ (70.1%),

What is Cloud Service?
It is a service that stores media files(photos, music, etc.) and personal files(documents, address books, etc.)
on a web server rather than an external storage space. The stored files can be downloaded to a computer,
smartphone, etc. for desired operations like editing, etc.
Example) Drive type (Naver Cloud, Google Drive, iCloud, KT Cloud, LG U+Box, MS OneDrive, Dropbox, etc.)
Document work (Google Docs, MS Office 365, etc.)
Schedule/Contact (Google Calendar, Naver Calendar, Naver Address Book, etc.)

K. AI Service Utilization Competency and Ethical Use
When asked about perceptions of AI service utilization competency and ethical use, the highest positive
perception(‘agree’ + ‘strongly agree’) was ‘I can use devices with AI technology in daily life’ at 45.0%, followed by ‘I can
use appropriate AI technologies to achieve daily goals(such as work, education, etc.)’ at 39.4%.

Among the population aged 3 or older, 5.5% are non-users of the Internet
5.5% of the population aged 3 or older (a decrease of 0.5%p from the previous year) were ‘Internet non-users’ who have
not used the Internet within the past 1 month. The proportion of non-users was higher among ‘Female’ (6.4%) than ‘Male’
(4.7%). By age group, nearly all individuals in their ‘10s’ to ‘50s’ were using the Internet, while the non-user rate was
relatively higher among those in their ‘70+’ (32.0%) and ‘60s’ (4.3%).

The main reason for not using the Internet is ‘No interest or not needed’ (76.2%)
The most common reason for not using the Internet was ‘No interest or not needed’ (76.2%), followed by ‘No confidence
in using it or do not know how to use it’ (56.5%). Other reasons for not using the Internet included ‘Cost of using it is
burdensome’ (11.1%), ‘Due to lack of equipment like computer’ (8.2%), ‘Because content may be harmful’ (3.7%), etc.

30.1% of Internet non-users are willing to use the Internet
The future intention of Internet use among non-Internet users was 30.1%. By age group, it was relatively low at 18.5%
for those ‘70s or older’, 45.2% for those in their ‘60s’, and 56.3% for those in their ‘50s’. This suggests that the future
intention of Internet use among the elderly is generally low.
